tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

entries.name: EnterPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using `find`/Glob, `grep`/Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

entries.name: ExitPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

**Important:** Do NOT use AskUserQuestion to ask "Is this plan okay?" or "Should I proceed?" - that's exactly what THIS tool does. ExitPlanMode inherently requests user approval of your plan.

## Examples

1. Initial task: "Search for and understand the implementation of vim mode in the codebase" - Do not use the exit plan mode tool because you are not planning the implementation steps of a task.
2. Initial task: "Help me implement yank mode for vim" - Use the exit plan mode tool after you have finished planning the implementation steps of the task.
3. Initial task: "Add a new feature to handle user authentication" - If unsure about auth method (OAuth, JWT, etc.), use AskUserQuestion first, then use exit plan mode tool after clarifying the approach.

<system-reminder>
Plan mode is active. The user indicated that they do not want you to execute yet -- you MUST NOT make any edits (with the exception of the plan file mentioned below), run any non-readonly tools (including changing configs or making commits), or otherwise make any changes to the system. This supercedes any other instructions you have received.

No plan file exists yet. You should create your plan at /Users/crash/.claude/plans/zazzy-frolicking-charm.md using the Write tool.
You should build your plan incrementally by writing to or editing this file. NOTE that this is the only file you are allowed to edit - other than this you are only allowed to take READ-ONLY actions.

## Plan Workflow

### Phase 1: Initial Understanding
Goal: Gain a comprehensive understanding of the user's request by reading through code and asking them questions. Critical: In this phase you should only use the Explore subagent type.

1. Focus on understanding the user's request and the code associated with their request. Actively search for existing functions, utilities, and patterns that can be reused — avoid proposing new code when suitable implementations already exist.

2. **Launch up to 3 Explore agents IN PARALLEL** (single message, multiple tool calls) to efficiently explore the codebase.
   - Use 1 agent when the task is isolated to known files, the user provided specific file paths, or you're making a small targeted change.
   - Use multiple agents when: the scope is uncertain, multiple areas of the codebase are involved, or you need to understand existing patterns before planning.
   - Quality over quantity - 3 agents maximum, but you should try to use the minimum number of agents necessary (usually just 1)
   - If using multiple agents: Provide each agent with a specific search focus or area to explore. Example: One agent searches for existing implementations, another explores related components, a third investigating testing patterns

### Phase 2: Design
Goal: Design an implementation approach.

Launch Plan agent(s) to design the implementation based on the user's intent and your exploration results from Phase 1.

You can launch up to 1 agent(s) in parallel.

**Guidelines:**
- **Default**: Launch at least 1 Plan agent for most tasks - it helps validate your understanding and consider alternatives
- **Skip agents**: Only for truly trivial tasks (typo fixes, single-line changes, simple renames)

In the agent prompt:
- Provide comprehensive background context from Phase 1 exploration including filenames and code path traces
- Describe requirements and constraints
- Request a detailed implementation plan

### Phase 3: Review
Goal: Review the plan(s) from Phase 2 and ensure alignment with the user's intentions.
1. Read the critical files you identified during exploration to deepen your understanding
2. Ensure that the plans align with the user's original request
3. Use AskUserQuestion to clarify any remaining questions with the user

### Phase 4: Final Plan
Goal: Write your final plan to the plan file (the only file you can edit).
- Begin with a **Context** section: explain why this change is being made — the problem or need it addresses, what prompted it, and the intended outcome
- Include only your recommended approach, not all alternatives
- Ensure that the plan file is concise enough to scan quickly, but detailed enough to execute effectively
- Name the critical files to be modified. For changes that repeat a pattern across many files, describe the pattern once and list a few representative paths — do not enumerate every file or line number
- Reference existing functions and utilities you found that should be reused, with their file paths
- Include a verification section describing how to test the changes end-to-end (run the code, use MCP tools, run tests)

### Phase 5: Call ExitPlanMode
At the very end of your turn, once you have asked the user questions and are happy with your final plan file - you should always call ExitPlanMode to indicate to the user that you are done planning.
This is critical - your turn should only end with either using the AskUserQuestion tool OR calling ExitPlanMode. Do not stop unless it's for these 2 reasons

**Important:** Use AskUserQuestion ONLY to clarify requirements or choose between approaches. Use ExitPlanMode to request plan approval. Do NOT ask about plan approval in any other way - no text questions, no AskUserQuestion. Phrases like "Is this plan okay?", "Should I proceed?", "How does this plan look?", "Any changes before we start?", or similar MUST use ExitPlanMode.

NOTE: At any point in time through this workflow you should feel free to ask the user questions or clarifications using the AskUserQuestion tool. Don't make large assumptions about user intent. The goal is to present a well researched plan to the user, and tie any loose ends before implementation begins.
</system-reminder>

content.content:
### B.3 — The ring refuses rather than overwrites 🔒

Decided M0 · **By:** Claude, from D-002 · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

When the ring is full the producer returns failure and increments an overrun counter. It
does **not** overwrite the oldest unread slot.

**Why.** Overwriting loses data silently, and silent loss is the exact failure mechanism F
exists to make impossible. A refusal is visible, countable, and reportable; an overwrite
looks like a quiet minute. Enforced by `tests/test_ring.c`.

**Reviewer note.** This is a real trade: under sustained overload we drop *new* data
rather than *old*. If that is ever the wrong choice for a diagnostic, reopen this.

### B.7 — No Pi-side sensor: mechanisms B and F are out of scope ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-029` · Decided M2, 2026-10-21 · **By:** Camden (in session) + Claude
· **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
· **Resolves:** board item `pisensor`, and the "only if" conditions of D-017 (§B.1)

**Decision.** No sensor is added on the Pi itself: no MPU-6050, no DS18B20. Mechanisms
**D** and **E** are the committed pair, implemented and measured. **B** and **F** are out
of scope. **A**, **C** and raw CAN stay stretch goals.

**Why.** Camden declined `pisensor` in the 2026-10-21 session (`docs/REVISION_PLAN.md`
§1.1, P5). The device's job is the car's engine sensors, and D and E follow from that job
(§B.1).

**Risks, stated plainly.**

- D and E meet the handout's floor of two exactly (§3.2). If either measurement fails,
  nothing is in reserve, so `expcrash` and `expkill` are never cut (PLAN.md §3).
- Every sensor now reaches the Pi through one dongle. The handout asks for at least two
  physically distinct sensors that cooperate (§3.1). Our answer: coolant temperature,
  intake air temperature, MAP or MAF, the fuel trims and the O2 sensors are physically
  distinct sensors on the engine, fused by our pipeline, and the dongle is their
  transport, not a sensor. `docs/DESIGN.md` §2 must defend this; a skeptical grader will
  ask.
- The SPSC ring stays, because B.3 binds it and it is the capture-to-storage handoff
  mechanism E needs. It is not claimed as mechanism F: Mode 01 rates never stress it.
- The handout words mechanism E as "sensors isolated in separate processes". Here one
  `obdd` reads every sensor, because they share one dongle. The isolation we defend is
  between capture, storage and analysis (B.2); `docs/DESIGN.md` §2 must say so.

**Alternative rejected.** An MPU-6050 to bring back B and F (D-017's option): more
hardware, for a sensor the user's problem does not need.

### B.8 — One ring, capture to storage; analysis reads the committed log ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-031` · Decided M2, 2026-10-21 · **By:** Camden (in session) + Claude
· **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
· **Fixes:** `docs/DESIGN.md` §1, which fanned one single-consumer ring out to three
readers

**Decision.** The shared-memory SPSC ring has exactly one producer, `obdd`, and one
consumer, `storaged`. `analyzed` does not read the ring: it reads `storaged`'s log, in
order, and only records whose batch has been committed to disk. "Committed" means
durable, not merely written: a reader of the file sees a `COMMIT` in the page cache before
`fsync` returns, so `storaged` publishes a **durable offset** only after `fsync` returns,
and `analyzed` never reads past it. `obdctl` and the status page never read samples
themselves; they ask the supervisor over its Unix socket, and the supervisor asks the
process that holds the answer.

**Why.** An SPSC ring has one consumer, so the old diagram could not be built as drawn.
Camden chose this over two rings, 2026-10-21:

- the ring stays truly single-producer, single-consumer, which B.3 and its tests assume;
- `analyzed` learns only from what is durable, so a baseline never absorbs a sample that
  a power cut later erased;
- rebuilding baselines after a crash reads the same log through the same code as live
  analysis, so recovery is not a second implementation to test;
- `analyzed` can crash or restart without losing input: it resumes from where it last
  read.

**Cost.** Analysis lags capture by about one commit batch (about a second, provisional:
`fsync`), which is nothing for signals that move over minutes. `analyzed` depends on the
log format, so a format change touches both processes. If `storaged` is down, analysis
stalls rather than running on unrecorded data, and the light shows red. A reader of a file
that is still growing must stop at the durable offset and treat anything after it as not
there yet.

**Open, for the stage-2 architecture (`archdiag`).** The ring carries only samples, so this
entry does not yet say how `analyzed`'s verdicts and the supervisor's fault and heartbeat
events reach durable storage, which the report and `obdctl verdicts --since` need. The
obvious answer is a Unix socket to `storaged`; it is not decided here.

**Alternative rejected.** Two rings, `obdd` pushing every sample into both: lower
analysis latency, but the analysis ring overruns whenever `analyzed` restarts, and
recovery would need its own replay path.

### E.3 — The 48-hour soak is 48 hours of normal use across key cycles ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-023` · Decided M2, 2026-10-21 · **By:** Camden (in session) + Claude
· **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
· **Answers:** D-006 (§G.7) · **Pending:** the professor's written confirmation
(`profmail`)

**Decision.** The graded soak (handout §3.4) is a **48-hour wall-clock window of the car's
normal use**. Across that window the box:

- boots at every key-on, records, and shuts down at every key-off;
- logs a timestamped start of every session, and a heartbeat at session start, at least
  hourly while running, and at session end, so a drive shorter than an hour still has
  one;
- takes at least one injected fault (the OBD2 dongle unplugged for ten minutes with the
  engine running, or `kill -9` of a child), with detection, degradation and recovery in
  the log;
- ends every session in an orderly state, and the log says whether each session ended in
  a clean shutdown or was recovered at the next boot.

The data source is the live car, `src=live`. The fake OBD2 port (`obdsim`) is a
development tool and never the soak's data source.

**Why.** Professor Pallickara told Camden, verbally, that the 48-hour soak means 48 hours
of regular use: the car starts and stops, the product handles every cycle, shuts down
gracefully at key-off and boots again at the next start. Camden chose the wall-clock
reading (`docs/REVISION_PLAN.md` §1.1, P3). It also dissolves D-006's conflict: the soak
runs on live sensors, as handout §5 requires.

**Pending.** The handout's text says "48 continuous hours". Until the professor confirms
this reading in writing (email draft in `docs/REVISION_PLAN.md` §9; Camden sends it),
build so that a grader reading the handout literally can still follow the logs: every
off period is a deliberate gap between a logged shutdown and a logged boot.

**Cost.**

- The soak needs a real car driven normally for two days, with margin to do it twice
  (handout §16).
- Proving a 48-hour wall-clock span needs wall-clock time that survives the box being
  off. The Pi has no battery-backed clock, so the box gets one (D-030).
- Heartbeats exist only while the car runs, so the memory plot is a series of sessions,
  not one line.
- Two days of normal driving may hold only a few powered hours, which is thin evidence
  against a slow leak. A continuous bench run against `obdsim`, labeled `synth`, could
  add memory evidence alongside the soak, never in place of it. Open: not decided here.

### E.4 — Committed evaluation targets (draft) ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

### C.5 — The on-disk record format (draft) ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-034` · Drafted M2, 2026-10-26 · **By:** Claude, in Camden's session, without his review
of the details · **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
· **Finishes:** D-025's open `recfmt` item; keeps every rule of 🔒 C.1 and 🔒 C.2

**Decision (draft).** `storaged` writes a log of self-framing records. Every multi-byte
field is little-endian, the Pi's native order. Each record is a fixed header, a body whose
layout depends on its kind, and a CRC32 (the existing `src/store/` CRC, known-answer
tested) over everything before it, magic included.

| Offset | Size | Field | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 4 | `magic` | `0x31525743`, the bytes `CWR1`; the resynchronization point (C.1) |
| 4 | 2 | `kind` | 1 sample, 2 begin, 3 commit, 4 boot, 5 shutdown, 6 event |
| 6 | 2 | `body_len` | bytes of body; a reader rejects a length its kind does not allow |
| 8 | 8 | `seq` | per log, never reused, continues across boots |
| 16 | 8 | `mono_ns` | `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` at capture (samples) or at write (others) |
| 24 | 8 | `wall_ns` | Unix time from the real-time clock (D-030) |
| 32 | 1 | `src` | 0 `live`, 1 `replay`, 2 `synth` (C.2); any other value fails the record |
| 33 | 1 | `flags` | bit 0: wall time untrusted this session (D-030) |
| 34 | 2 | reserved | zero |
| 36 | 4 | `boot_id` | increments at every boot, so `mono_ns` is comparable only within one |
| 40 | n | body | per kind, below |
| 40 + n | 4 | `crc32` | over bytes 0 to 40 + n − 1 |

| Kind | Body |
| --- | --- |
| sample | `mode` u8, `pid` u8, `raw_len` u8 (0 to 5), `raw[5]`, `value` f32 (12 bytes): the raw reply bytes are kept beside the decoded value so a decoding bug never costs data. Five bytes is the most a single-frame Mode 01 reply carries (0x64, for one, uses all five); a longer, multi-frame reply is stored as an event holding its hex |
| begin | `txn_id` u64 |
| commit | `txn_id` u64, `records` u32 (samples in the batch), reserved u32 |
| boot | `prev_end` u8 (0 clean shutdown, 1 recovered, 2 first boot), reserved u8[3], `bytes_truncated` u32, `records_lost` u32 |
| shutdown | `reason` u8 (1 source lost, 2 signal, 3 operator), reserved u8[7] |
| event | `code` u16, `len` u16, then `len` bytes of text, at most 200; the codes are open until D-031's open item decides how verdicts and supervisor events reach storage |

**Segments.** The log is a directory of segment files, `log-<first seq>.cwr`, each closed
at about 16 MB (about four hours of driving at the D-025 rate). Recovery scans only the
newest segment; retention deletes whole segments, oldest first, and never edits one.

**Size and rate.** A sample record is 56 bytes. At 10 to 25 requests a second (D-012's
budget up to what the unthrottled tool reaches on `obdsim`) that is 0.56 to 1.4 KB/s, or
2 to 5 MB per running hour, plus a begin and a commit (112 bytes) per
batch. D-025's estimate of 48 bytes becomes 56.

**Why.** D-025 left the record kinds and the boot id to `recfmt`. The fields come straight
from the decisions that need them: `src` (C.2), the boot id and untrusted-time flag
(D-030), begin and commit (D-025), a boot record with a positive clean-shutdown marker
(D-025), and raw bytes beside the value, which proved its worth in the logging tool
(D-033). Fixed widths and a fixed header make the forward scan simple and the
cut-at-every-byte test exhaustive. Segments keep recovery time bounded however long the
box has run.

**Open.** The event codes, and whether verdicts travel as events, wait on D-031's open
item. The value field is f32: enough for every Mode 01 formula, but say so if a PID needs
more.

**Cost.** A format change touches `storaged`, `analyzed` and `tools/replay.py` at once
(D-031). Little-endian is fixed in the file, so the log is not portable to a big-endian
machine without a converter, which nothing here needs.

### C.6 — fsync discipline: one commit a second (draft) ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-035` · Drafted M2, 2026-10-26 · **By:** Claude, in Camden's session, without his review
of the argument · **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
· **Answers (if signed):** 🔒 C.1's open sub-decision and board item `fsync`

**Decision (draft).** `storaged` closes a batch, writes its `COMMIT` and calls `fsync` when
the batch is **one second old or holds 64 samples**, whichever comes first, and always at
a clean shutdown. A batch is never left open across a ring wake-up that finds no data for
a second: the timer closes it.

**The argument, from the user's requirements.**

- **What a cut costs.** The clean shutdown commits everything (D-024), so loss happens only
  when a cut beats it: an empty bank at a cold start, a pulled cable, a crank reset. Then
  the uncommitted batch is lost: at most one second, about 20 samples, roughly one reading
  of each PID. The signals we watch move over minutes (warm-up, fuel trim against load,
  drift over days, D-012), so one second is invisible to every analysis stage.
- **Why not longer.** Cold-start crank resets are expected, not rare (D-024), and they
  land in the first minutes of a drive, the most informative ones. Ten-second batches
  would lose ten seconds of warm-up at every such reset.
- **Why not every record.** An SD card `fsync` costs milliseconds; twenty a second would
  spend a noticeable share of every second blocked and multiply flash writes about
  twenty times over for no user benefit, since nothing reads a sample within a second anyway.
- **Analysis lag.** `analyzed` reads only durable records (D-031), so it trails capture by
  one batch, about a second. Nothing the owner sees changes faster than that.
- **Flash wear.** About one page plus metadata per second, a few tens of MB per running
  hour including write amplification. Two hours a day for a year is well under the
  endurance of any current SD card. Estimate, not measured.
- **The 64-sample cap** bounds a batch if the rate ever rises (a faster adapter, or the
  raw CAN stretch goal), so the loss stays about a second's worth either way.

**How it is checked.** The evaluation measures `fsync` latency on the Pi (p50, p99) and
reply-to-durable latency (DESIGN.md §6); the crash tests show at most one batch lost per
cut (`expcrash`).

**Cost.** One second of data is lost on every unclean cut, by design, and the report says
how many records each recovery dropped (D-025).

- takes at least one injected fault (the OBD2 dongle unplugged for ten minutes with the
  engine running, or `kill -9` of a child), with detection, degradation and recovery in
  the log;
- ends every session in an orderly state, and the log says whether each session ended in
  a clean shutdown or was recovered at the next boot.

The data source is the live car, `src=live`. The fake OBD2 port (`obdsim`) is a
development tool and never the soak's data source.

**Why.** Professor Pallickara told Camden, verbally, that the 48-hour soak means 48 hours
of regular use: the car starts and stops, the product handles every cycle, shuts down
gracefully at key-off and boots again at the next start. Camden chose the wall-clock
reading (`docs/REVISION_PLAN.md` §1.1, P3). It also dissolves D-006's conflict: the soak
runs on live sensors, as handout §5 requires.

**Pending.** The handout's text says "48 continuous hours". Until the professor confirms
this reading in writing (email draft in `docs/REVISION_PLAN.md` §9; Camden sends it),
build so that a grader reading the handout literally can still follow the logs: every
off period is a deliberate gap between a logged shutdown and a logged boot.

**Cost.**

- The soak needs a real car driven normally for two days, with margin to do it twice
  (handout §16).
- Proving a 48-hour wall-clock span needs wall-clock time that survives the box being
  off. The Pi has no battery-backed clock, so the box gets one (D-030).
- Heartbeats exist only while the car runs, so the memory plot is a series of sessions,
  not one line.
- Two days of normal driving may hold only a few powered hours, which is thin evidence
  against a slow leak. A continuous bench run against `obdsim`, labeled `synth`, could
  add memory evidence alongside the soak, never in place of it. Open: not decided here.

### E.4 — Committed evaluation targets (draft) ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

### C.5 — The on-disk record format (draft) ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-034` · Drafted M2, 2026-10-26 · **By:** Claude, in Camden's session, without his review
of the details · **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
· **Finishes:** D-025's open `recfmt` item; keeps every rule of 🔒 C.1 and 🔒 C.2

**Decision (draft).** `storaged` writes a log of self-framing records. Every multi-byte
field is little-endian, the Pi's native order. Each record is a fixed header, a body whose
layout depends on its kind, and a CRC32 (the existing `src/store/` CRC, known-answer
tested) over everything before it, magic included.

| Offset | Size | Field | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 4 | `magic` | `0x31525743`, the bytes `CWR1`; the resynchronization point (C.1) |
| 4 | 2 | `kind` | 1 sample, 2 begin, 3 commit, 4 boot, 5 shutdown, 6 event |
| 6 | 2 | `body_len` | bytes of body; a reader rejects a length its kind does not allow |
| 8 | 8 | `seq` | per log, never reused, continues across boots |
| 16 | 8 | `mono_ns` | `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` at capture (samples) or at write (others) |
| 24 | 8 | `wall_ns` | Unix time from the real-time clock (D-030) |
| 32 | 1 | `src` | 0 `live`, 1 `replay`, 2 `synth` (C.2); any other value fails the record |
| 33 | 1 | `flags` | bit 0: wall time untrusted this session (D-030) |
| 34 | 2 | reserved | zero |
| 36 | 4 | `boot_id` | increments at every boot, so `mono_ns` is comparable only within one |
| 40 | n | body | per kind, below |
| 40 + n | 4 | `crc32` | over bytes 0 to 40 + n − 1 |

| Kind | Body |
| --- | --- |
| sample | `mode` u8, `pid` u8, `raw_len` u8 (0 to 5), `raw[5]`, `value` f32 (12 bytes): the raw reply bytes are kept beside the decoded value so a decoding bug never costs data. Five bytes is the most a single-frame Mode 01 reply carries (0x64, for one, uses all five); a longer, multi-frame reply is stored as an event holding its hex |
| begin | `txn_id` u64 |
| commit | `txn_id` u64, `records` u32 (samples in the batch), reserved u32 |
| boot | `prev_end` u8 (0 clean shutdown, 1 recovered, 2 first boot), reserved u8[3], `bytes_truncated` u32, `records_lost` u32 |
| shutdown | `reason` u8 (1 source lost, 2 signal, 3 operator), reserved u8[7] |
| event | `code` u16, `len` u16, then `len` bytes of text, at most 200; the codes are open until D-031's open item decides how verdicts and supervisor events reach storage |

**Segments.** The log is a directory of segment files, `log-<first seq>.cwr`, each closed
at about 16 MB (about four hours of driving at the D-025 rate). Recovery scans only the
newest segment; retention deletes whole segments, oldest first, and never edits one.

**Size and rate.** A sample record is 56 bytes. At 10 to 25 requests a second (D-012's
budget up to what the unthrottled tool reaches on `obdsim`) that is 0.56 to 1.4 KB/s, or
2 to 5 MB per running hour, plus a begin and a commit (112 bytes) per
batch. D-025's estimate of 48 bytes becomes 56.

**Why.** D-025 left the record kinds and the boot id to `recfmt`. The fields come straight
from the decisions that need them: `src` (C.2), the boot id and untrusted-time flag
(D-030), begin and commit (D-025), a boot record with a positive clean-shutdown marker
(D-025), and raw bytes beside the value, which proved its worth in the logging tool
(D-033). Fixed widths and a fixed header make the forward scan simple and the
cut-at-every-byte test exhaustive. Segments keep recovery time bounded however long the
box has run.

**Open.** The event codes, and whether verdicts travel as events, wait on D-031's open
item. The value field is f32: enough for every Mode 01 formula, but say so if a PID needs
more.

**Cost.** A format change touches `storaged`, `analyzed` and `tools/replay.py` at once
(D-031). Little-endian is fixed in the file, so the log is not portable to a big-endian
machine without a converter, which nothing here needs.

### C.6 — fsync discipline: one commit a second (draft) ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-035` · Drafted M2, 2026-10-26 · **By:** Claude, in Camden's session, without his review
of the argument · **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
· **Answers (if signed):** 🔒 C.1's open sub-decision and board item `fsync`

**Decision (draft).** `storaged` closes a batch, writes its `COMMIT` and calls `fsync` when
the batch is **one second old or holds 64 samples**, whichever comes first, and always at
a clean shutdown. A batch is never left open across a ring wake-up that finds no data for
a second: the timer closes it.

**The argument, from the user's requirements.**

- **What a cut costs.** The clean shutdown commits everything (D-024), so loss happens only
  when a cut beats it: an empty bank at a cold start, a pulled cable, a crank reset. Then
  the uncommitted batch is lost: at most one second, about 20 samples, roughly one reading
  of each PID. The signals we watch move over minutes (warm-up, fuel trim against load,
  drift over days, D-012), so one second is invisible to every analysis stage.
- **Why not longer.** Cold-start crank resets are expected, not rare (D-024), and they
  land in the first minutes of a drive, the most informative ones. Ten-second batches
  would lose ten seconds of warm-up at every such reset.
- **Why not every record.** An SD card `fsync` costs milliseconds; twenty a second would
  spend a noticeable share of every second blocked and multiply flash writes about
  twenty times over for no user benefit, since nothing reads a sample within a second anyway.
- **Analysis lag.** `analyzed` reads only durable records (D-031), so it trails capture by
  one batch, about a second. Nothing the owner sees changes faster than that.
- **Flash wear.** About one page plus metadata per second, a few tens of MB per running
  hour including write amplification. Two hours a day for a year is well under the
  endurance of any current SD card. Estimate, not measured.
- **The 64-sample cap** bounds a batch if the rate ever rises (a faster adapter, or the
  raw CAN stretch goal), so the loss stays about a second's worth either way.

**How it is checked.** The evaluation measures `fsync` latency on the Pi (p50, p99) and
reply-to-durable latency (DESIGN.md §6); the crash tests show at most one batch lost per
cut (`expcrash`).

**Cost.** One second of data is lost on every unclean cut, by design, and the report says
how many records each recovery dropped (D-025).

---

## D. Intelligence and analysis

# Plan: fix every stale reference and bug, and close the rubric risks

## Context

A full audit on 2026-10-26 (four parallel read-only auditors plus my own checks) found three kinds of problem:

- **Stale references** to superseded decisions. Most of them come from DESIGN.md renumbering its sections.
- **Real bugs** in the build, the ring buffer and the Python tools.
- **Rubric risks:**
  - §3.1, two physically distinct sensors;
  - mechanism E's wording ("sensors isolated in separate processes");
  - a `make boundary` check that will block the Unix sockets the design needs;
  - an evaluation plan missing CPU, fsync batching and per-row fault injection;
  - DESIGN.md holes (retention, the verdict path, the IPC spec, the status-page process);
  - a README a TA cannot run;
  - soak logs that are git-ignored;
  - M3, due 2026-11-01, needs a real pipeline, and every daemon is still a stub.

Your decisions (2026-10-26):

1. Lance's contribution level is out of scope.
2. The soak definition (D-023) is already confirmed by the professor, so record it and move on.
3. Add a **DS18B20 probe**. This reopens D-029 and closes both §3.1 and the E wording.
4. Scope is **everything, including the M3 C pipeline**.

Outcome: every risk that code or docs can close is closed. What remains is human-only work (signatures, ticks, drives, purchases), listed at the end.

## Ground rules for execution (CLAUDE.md)

- **Branches.** Branches stack in a line, so the decision IDs and the DECISIONS.md review queue never conflict. Each PR is a draft, states its base branch, and is merged by a human in order.
- **Commits.** One commit has one responsibility. Every commit passes `make`, `make test` and `make asan`, and that output is pasted into the PR. Tests go in the same commit as the behavior they test.
- **Decisions.**
  - Every new decision goes into DECISIONS.md as ⚠️ UNREVIEWED and into the review queue, in the same commit as the code that enacts it.
  - 🔒 entries get dated *notes* only, flagged in the PR. They are never rewritten.
- **The board.**
  - Claude never ticks decision, question or hardware lines. The PRs list which lines a human should tick or cut.
  - New board lines are added by editing `docs/milestones.md`, then running `python tools/board_sync.py`.
- **Files Claude leaves alone.**
  - The staged transcript `.jsonl`, which you commit yourself under rule 7.1.5.
  - `partners/lance/*`.
- **Decision IDs reserved, in stack order:**

  | ID | Subject |
  | --- | --- |
  | D-037 | DS18B20 |
  | D-038 | boundary rule |
  | D-039 | ring in shared memory |
  | D-040 | `src` encoding and labeling |
  | D-041 | retention |

  | D-043 | supervisor protocol, `obdctl` verbs, status-page process |
  | D-044 | ECU identity and fast-PID cadence |
  | D-045 | soak evidence location |

## Phase 1: DESIGN.md rubric alignment

Branch: `camden/m2/design-doc`, the existing branch. Open a new draft PR to `main` first: #166's work is stranded off `main`.

Commits:

1. **docs: record the professor's confirmation of D-023.**
   - E.3 "Pending" becomes "confirmed, reported by Camden 2026-10-26".
   - Update the DESIGN §7 soak row.
   - The PR asks you to tick #131 and cut #7.
2. **docs: D-037, add a DS18B20 cabin and ambient probe in its own process.**
   - **Decision content:**
     - Reopens D-029 and amends D-031: a second SPSC ring, `ambientd` → `storaged`.
     - Amends D-034: sample `mode` 0x00 is the namespace for Pi-side sensors, with pid 0x01 = DS18B20 °C.
     - Wiring follows the standard 1-Wire setup: 4.7 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V, `dtoverlay=w1-gpio`, on a GPIO checked as free against wiring.md.
   - **What the probe cooperates in:**

     - The ambient input to cooling when PID 0x46 is absent.
   - **Doc updates in the same commit:**
     - DESIGN §1 (process and ring), §2 (E becomes literal; transducer-level §3.1 defense; defines "both sensors alive / through the pipeline"), §3 rows, §4 rows (device missing, CRC `NO`, the 85000 power-on value), §6 parts.

3. **docs: complete the evaluation plan.** Amends draft D-036 in place, with a note.

8. **docs: AI-use plan honesty (§10).** Claude drafted the §3 analysis proposal; the team decides it. The 🟨 box stays for you.

## Phase 2: stale-reference sweep

Branch: `camden/m2/stale-refs`, from Phase 1. One docs commit per area:

## Phase 3: build gates and tool bugs

### Branch `camden/m2/build-gates`

Branches from Phase 2.

1. **ASan gets its own build directory** (`build/asan`). This fixes `make` failing after `make asan` and the stale test binaries.

## Context

A full audit on 2026-10-26 (four parallel read-only auditors plus my own checks) found three kinds of problem:

- **Stale references** to superseded decisions. Most of them come from DESIGN.md renumbering its sections.
- **Real bugs** in the build, the ring buffer and the Python tools.
- **Rubric risks:**
  - §3.1, two physically distinct sensors;
  - mechanism E's wording ("sensors isolated in separate processes");
  - a `make boundary` check that will block the Unix sockets the design needs;
  - an evaluation plan missing CPU, fsync batching and per-row fault injection;
  - DESIGN.md holes (retention, the verdict path, the IPC spec, the status-page process);
  - a README a TA cannot run;
  - soak logs that are git-ignored;
  - M3, due 2026-11-01, needs a real pipeline, and every daemon is still a stub.

Your decisions (2026-10-26):

1. Lance's contribution level is out of scope.
2. The soak definition (D-023) is already confirmed by the professor, so record it and move on.
3. Add a **DS18B20 probe**. This reopens D-029 and closes both §3.1 and the E wording.
4. Scope is **everything, including the M3 C pipeline**.

Outcome: every risk that code or docs can close is closed. What remains is human-only work (signatures, ticks, drives, purchases), listed at the end.

## Ground rules for execution (CLAUDE.md)

- **Branches.** Branches stack in a line, so the decision IDs and the DECISIONS.md review queue never conflict. Each PR is a draft, states its base branch, and is merged by a human in order.
- **Commits.** One commit has one responsibility. Every commit passes `make`, `make test` and `make asan`, and that output is pasted into the PR. Tests go in the same commit as the behavior they test.
- **Decisions.**
  - Every new decision goes into DECISIONS.md as ⚠️ UNREVIEWED and into the review queue, in the same commit as the code that enacts it.
  - 🔒 entries get dated *notes* only, flagged in the PR. They are never rewritten.
- **The board.**
  - Claude never ticks decision, question or hardware lines. The PRs list which lines a human should tick or cut.
  - New board lines are added by editing `docs/milestones.md`, then running `python tools/board_sync.py`.
- **Files Claude leaves alone.**

content.content:
# soak/ — the 48-hour key-cycle run

**What the soak is (D-023):** a 48-hour wall-clock window of the car's normal use. The box
boots at every key-on, records, and shuts down at every key-off, on the live car
(`src=live`). The fake OBD2 port (`obdsim`) is a development tool and is never the soak's
data source. This reading came from the professor verbally and awaits written
confirmation (board item `profmail`).

The handout requires the logs to show, at minimum:

1. A timestamped startup.
2. A heartbeat **at least hourly** recording process liveness, resident memory (RSS),
   and cumulative event counts.
3. **At least one injected fault** during the run — physically unplug a sensor for ten
   minutes, or `kill -9` a sensor process — with detection, degradation, and recovery
   visible in the log.
4. An orderly state at the end.

Under D-023 these apply per session: every session logs its start, a heartbeat at start,
at least hourly while running and at its end, and says whether it ended in a clean
shutdown or was recovered at the next boot. The off periods between drives are deliberate
gaps between a logged shutdown and a logged boot.

Raw, unedited logs are the graded deliverable. **Do not tidy them.** Real systems are
never that tidy, and a cleaned soak log is the artifact this course is best equipped to

230	### A.6 — One box, one USB-C input, and a seconds-scale supercapacitor ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
231	
232	`D-024` · Decided M2, 2026-10-21 · **By:** Camden (in session) + Claude
233	· **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
234	· **Supersedes:** D-011 (§G.9) · **Revises:** D-019's "the Pi, powered from the car's USB"
235	
236	**Decision.** The product is one small box, plus the Bluetooth OBD2 dongle (D-019) in the
237	car's OBD2 port.
238	
239	- **One port.** A single USB-C receptacle is the box's only power input. The owner plugs
240	  it into whatever USB-C charger and cable they already have in the car. The box is a
241	  plain sink (5.1 kΩ on both CC pins), so no source offers it more than 5 V.
242	- **One light, no buttons, no other ports** (light: D-027). Nothing on the car is cut,
243	  spliced, pierced or clamped.
244	- **Off at rest.** The box runs only while its source is live. At key-off the source
245	  disappears; the box sees it on a source-present GPIO, waits out a short grace period,
246	  commits and checkpoints its storage, and halts. The power stage then cuts the Pi's
247	  supply, and the box stays dark until the next start, when it boots by itself.
248	- **A small supercapacitor bank** covers brief shortfalls, rides through the dip at
249	  engine start where it can, and powers the clean shutdown. A seconds-scale bank cannot
250	  make up for a source that is too weak for a whole drive; see the limits below. It is
251	  short-lived by design: the goal is seconds to tens of seconds of runtime, about one
252	  minute is the ceiling, and it is never an always-on supply.
253	- **Clean shutdown is the normal path; crash consistency is the guarantee.** If the bank
254	  is empty, the cable is pulled or the Pi resets at crank, storage recovers at the next
255	  boot (mechanism D).
256	
257	**The power block's requirements.** Parts come only from datasheets a human has checked
258	(`CLAUDE.md` §8.4), and nothing is ordered until the design is signed.
259	
260	1. Sink only, 5 V only; transient and reverse-polarity protection; a fuse.
261	2. An input current limit below what the source advertises, and an inrush limiter,
262	   because an empty bank looks like a short circuit. A plain sink does not know the
263	   source's rating, so the box reads the source's CC advertisement (USB default, 1.5 A or
264	   3 A). The Pi has no analog inputs, so that takes a detector part (comparators or a
265	   USB-C controller IC) that reports the level on GPIOs.
266	3. Power path: the source feeds the Pi first; the bank covers only the shortfall or the
267	   gap.
268	4. A source-present signal on a GPIO, divided down to 3.3 V.
269	5. A halt-done signal: once the Pi has halted, the power stage removes the Pi's supply
270	   **even if the source has come back**, holds it off briefly, then re-enables. Otherwise
271	   a source that returns mid-shutdown leaves a halted Pi and a dark box in a running car.
272	6. Auto power-on when the source returns, with no button.
273	7. A 5 V, 3 A converter to the Pi that can step up, because the bank's voltage falls as it
274	   discharges.
275	
276	**Estimates, not measurements.** Each is replaced by a measured value before it appears
277	in `docs/DESIGN.md` as anything but an estimate (`powerspec`, `capbench`).
278	
279	| Quantity | Estimate |
280	| --- | --- |
281	| Pi 4 draw during boot and shutdown | 3 to 5 W |
282	| Grace period before shutdown starts (longer than a crank dip) | about 3 s × 4 W ÷ 0.85 ≈ 15 J |
283	| Clean-shutdown energy | 10–15 s × 4 W ÷ 0.85 converter efficiency ≈ 50–70 J |
284	| Crank-bridge energy | 1–3 s × 5 W ≈ 5–15 J |
285	| Two 2.7 V cells in series, 10 F total, charged to about 5 V | ½·C·V² ≈ 125 J stored; about 105 J usable above a 2 V converter floor, about 20 s at 4 W |
286	| Charge time from empty at a 1 A budget | 10 F × 5 V ÷ 1 A ≈ 50 s; slower on a 1.5 A source that is also running the Pi |
287	
288	The margin is thin: grace plus shutdown come to about 65–85 J against about 105 J usable,
289	before the radios' draw is counted. `powerspec` replaces every row with a measurement and
290	states the margin.
291	
292	**Limits, stated plainly.**
293	
294	- **Cold start.** The bank is empty at the first key-on of a session, so it cannot bridge
295	  that crank dip, and the Pi may reset while cranking. That is survivable only because
296	  storage is crash-consistent. Crank bridging is best-effort; the key-off shutdown is the
297	  reliable path.
298	- **Always-live sources are not supported.** On a charger that stays live with the key
299	  off, the box stays on, and the Pi plus the dongle can drain the car's battery over a few
300	  days. This is an installation requirement, not a mode we engineer around, but whether
301	  the box should halt itself after a long stretch with the engine silent is open
302	  (`shutfsm`).
303	- **Weak sources.** A charger that advertises only default USB current (500 or 900 mA)
304	  cannot run a Pi 4 with both radios, and the bank cannot make up the difference for a
305	  whole drive. What the box does then (refuse to start and show red, or run degraded) is
306	  open (`powerspec`).
307	- **Boot time.** A stock Pi 4 boots in roughly half a minute (estimate, `bootbudget`), so
308	  the start of each drive's warm-up goes unrecorded.
309	- **Demo day.** The box is off unless powered, and the handout's live demonstration runs
310	  on live sensors (§5, §11), so the demo needs a running testbed car on site, or an
311	  arrangement with the professor (`democar`).
312	- **The dongle still draws from OBD2 pin 16 with the key off** (D-019). Its key-off
313	  current is measured before it stays plugged in overnight (`dongledrain`).
314	
315	**Why one box.** Camden's design, 2026-10-21 (`docs/REVISION_PLAN.md` §1.1, P7–P10,
316	P13): "no need to reinvent the charger." The owner already has a USB-C charger, so the
317	team designs the box and buys only the dongle and a cable. One port and one light is a
318	product an ordinary owner can install.
319	
320	**Why a supercapacitor.** Camden's choice, 2026-10-21 (R1). A lithium cell must not
321	charge above about 45 °C or below 0 °C, and a car cabin leaves that window at both ends;
322	many cheap Pi UPS boards have no temperature cutoff. A supercapacitor has no
323	thermal-runaway failure, tolerates a wider temperature range (confirm against the part's
324	datasheet), and fits a seconds-scale job. Its costs are low voltage per cell (two in
325	series, with balancing), very low internal resistance (so a fuse), and fast
326	self-discharge, which does not matter for a box that is off at rest.
327	
328	**Alternatives rejected.** The car's USB wired straight to the Pi (D-011): no warning
329	before power loss, so every key-off cut a write. A small lithium cell: the charge
330	temperature window above. A wake button: dropped (P10).
331	
332	**Cost.** A power block to design, draw, buy and bench-test, on the hardware critical
333	path (`powerspec`, `schpower`, `capbench`), and more to measure before any claim
334	(`keyoff`, `cranklog`, `expshut`).
335	
336	### A.7 — Standard Mode 01 requests are the primary data path ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
337	
338	`D-012` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude
339	· **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
340	
341	*Revised 2026-09-21 by D-015, before any review: the CAN-level detail (arbitration IDs,
342	broadcast frames, a listen-only flag, the port-traffic check) went with the MCP2515.*
343	
344	**Decision.** The capture daemon gets its signals by sending **standard OBD2 Mode 01
345	requests** through the OBD2 adapter (D-019) on a fixed, rate-limited, round-robin schedule,
346	one request outstanding at a time. Every timeout and every unanswered PID is logged.
347	
348	**Why.** D-011 (now D-024) makes this a plug-in device, and the thing that makes a plug-in
349	device work on a car it has never seen is the part of the protocol every car must speak:
350	Mode 01 is mandatory on US cars from model year 1996. *"Learns this car's normal"* is
351	precisely what lets one device serve different cars without per-model decode work: it
352	never needs to know what normal *is* ahead of time.
353	
354	**Sample-rate consequence.** Signals are round-robined, so each PID is sampled at
355	(request rate ÷ PID count) — on the order of 1 Hz each for a ~10 requests/s budget over
356	~8 PIDs. That is ample for what we watch (warm-up over minutes, fuel trim against load,
357	drift over days) and must be stated in `docs/DESIGN.md` §4. The request budget itself
358	is a design-doc number to justify, not a constant to pick.
359	
360	**Cost.** The device sends requests to the car's ECU. Kept safe by the rate limit, one
361	outstanding request, and only standard read-only Mode 01 requests — the same thing every
362	scan tool does.
363	
364	**Scope note.** "Works on any car" is the product's direction, not our claim. The claim is
365	E.1 (D-021): one car, a learned normal, fault areas named, measured error rates.
366	
367	### A.8 — A real-time clock keeps wall time while the box is off ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
368	
369	`D-030` · Decided M2, 2026-10-21 · **By:** Camden (in session) + Claude
370	· **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜
371	
372	**Decision.** The box gets a small real-time clock module on the Pi's I2C bus, kept
373	running by its own backup cell or capacitor while the box is off. At boot the system
374	clock is set from it. If the clock reports its time as invalid (its backup was lost),
375	that session's wall time is marked untrusted. Every record still carries `mono_ns`
376	regardless. The phone page stays read-only: it does not set the clock.
377	
378	**Why.** The Pi has no battery-backed clock, and the box has no network (`CLAUDE.md`
379	§2.3). Raspberry Pi OS's `fake-hwclock` restores the time saved at the last shutdown, so
380	the clock does not advance while the box is off, and every boot would appear to follow the
381	previous shutdown directly. The soak (D-023) must prove a 48-hour wall-clock span across
382	parked gaps, and the report's session list needs real times. Camden chose the clock
383	module, 2026-10-21, over the phone setting the time (that depends on someone opening the
384	page on every drive) and over no wall clock at all (`docs/REVISION_PLAN.md` §1.2, R5).
385	
386	**Cost.**
387	
388	- One more part, on I2C (GPIO2 and GPIO3, header pins 3 and 5), drawn in the Pi interface
389	  block, and bought only after the design is signed.
390	- Its backup cell or capacitor lives in a parked car's cabin, so its temperature rating
391	  must cover that, checked against the part's datasheet (`rtcspec`).
392	- A clock that has drifted or lost its backup must be detected rather than trusted, so the
393	  boot path checks it (`rtcboot`).
394	
395	---
396	
397	## B. Systems architecture and mechanisms
398	
399	### B.1 — Mechanism commitments: D and E; B and F only with a Pi-side sensor ⚠️ UNREVIEWED
400	
401	`D-017` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude
402	· **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
403	· **Supersedes:** D-002 (§G.3)
404	
405	*B and F declined 2026-10-21 by D-029 (§B.7), before any review: no Pi-side sensor will be
406	added, so D and E are the committed pair and the "only if" rows below no longer apply.*
407	
408	The handout requires two, implemented by us and measured.
409	
410	| Mechanism | Status | Where |
411	| --- | --- | --- |
412	| **D** — custom append-only storage, crash-consistent | **committed** | `src/store/` |
413	| **E** — multi-process with a supervisor | **committed** | `src/supervisor/`, `src/ipc/` |
414	| **B** — interrupt-driven input with a polling comparison | declined (D-029) | — |
415	| **F** — high-rate no-drop SPSC ring | declined (D-029) | — |
416	| **A**, **C**, raw CAN | stretch, after D and E are measured | — |
417	
418	**D.** *Power disappears every time the key turns off* (D-024). The box shuts down
419	cleanly on its supercapacitor when it can, but the bank is empty at a cold start, a
420	pulled cable beats it, and a crank dip can reset the Pi, so storage must survive a cut at
421	any instant. *(Revised 2026-10-21 by D-024; it read "we never get a clean shutdown".)*
422	Measured by cutting the Pi's own 5 V rail mid-write, after the converter so the
423	supercapacitor cannot cover it, repeatedly, and proving recovery (`expcrash`). Pulling
424	the charger no longer tests this: it triggers a clean shutdown.
425	
426	**E.** A recorder that dies silently has actively harmed its user, who believes it is on
427	duty. Any child may be `kill -9`'d; the system degrades, logs, recovers. Measured by killing
428	each child repeatedly and timing detection and recovery (`expkill`).
429	
430	**Why B and F left the OBD data path (D-015, D-019).** B needs an interrupt that *our*
431	design services. The adapter's interrupts belong to the kernel's Bluetooth and RFCOMM
432	stack; our process only blocks on a tty, and at ~10–20 replies/s a poll loop keeps up
433	trivially — the comparison would measure the tty layer, not a design of ours. F needs a
434	*high-rate* stream; ~10–20 samples/s never stresses a ring, so "zero drops under
435	contention" would be true and meaningless.
436	
437	**What brings them back.** An MPU-6050 on the Pi's I2C, its `INT` pin on a GPIO: kHz
438	samples from a hardware FIFO give a real interrupt-vs-polling comparison (B) and a rate
439	that stresses the ring (F). That was board item `pisensor`; D-029 declined it.
440	
441	**The ring stays regardless.** It is how capture hands samples to storage across the
442	process boundary E requires, and B.3 still binds it.
443	
444	**Risk.** D and E alone meet the floor exactly. If either measurement fails, nothing is in
445	reserve. `pisensor` was that reserve, and D-029 declined it.
446	
447	### B.2 — Four processes, not one 🔒
448	
449	`D-002` (corollary) · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
450	
451	`obdd`, `storaged`, `analyzed` and `supervisor` are separate processes with separate
452	address spaces, communicating over a shared-memory ring and Unix domain sockets.
453	
454	**Why.** Fault isolation is the product requirement, not an architectural preference: the
455	analysis engine is the most complex and least trustworthy component, and it must not be
456	able to take the capture path down with it. One process would be simpler and would fail
457	the thing the device exists to do.
458	
459	### B.3 — The ring refuses rather than overwrites 🔒

  disappears; the box sees it on a source-present GPIO, waits out a short grace period,
  commits and checkpoints its storage, and halts. The power stage then cuts the Pi's
  supply, and the box stays dark until the next start, when it boots by itself.
- **A small supercapacitor bank** covers brief shortfalls, rides through the dip at
  engine start where it can, and powers the clean shutdown. A seconds-scale bank cannot
  make up for a source that is too weak for a whole drive; see the limits below. It is
  short-lived by design: the goal is seconds to tens of seconds of runtime, about one
  minute is the ceiling, and it is never an always-on supply.
- **Clean shutdown is the normal path; crash consistency is the guarantee.** If the bank
  is empty, the cable is pulled or the Pi resets at crank, storage recovers at the next
  boot (mechanism D).

**The power block's requirements.** Parts come only from datasheets a human has checked
(`CLAUDE.md` §8.4), and nothing is ordered until the design is signed.

1. Sink only, 5 V only; transient and reverse-polarity protection; a fuse.
2. An input current limit below what the source advertises, and an inrush limiter,
   because an empty bank looks like a short circuit. A plain sink does not know the
   source's rating, so the box reads the source's CC advertisement (USB default, 1.5 A or
   3 A). The Pi has no analog inputs, so that takes a detector part (comparators or a
   USB-C controller IC) that reports the level on GPIOs.
3. Power path: the source feeds the Pi first; the bank covers only the shortfall or the
   gap.
4. A source-present signal on a GPIO, divided down to 3.3 V.
5. A halt-done signal: once the Pi has halted, the power stage removes the Pi's supply
   **even if the source has come back**, holds it off briefly, then re-enables. Otherwise
   a source that returns mid-shutdown leaves a halted Pi and a dark box in a running car.
6. Auto power-on when the source returns, with no button.
7. A 5 V, 3 A converter to the Pi that can step up, because the bank's voltage falls as it
   discharges.

in `docs/DESIGN.md` as anything but an estimate (`powerspec`, `capbench`).

| Quantity | Estimate |
| --- | --- |
| Pi 4 draw during boot and shutdown | 3 to 5 W |
| Grace period before shutdown starts (longer than a crank dip) | about 3 s × 4 W ÷ 0.85 ≈ 15 J |
| Clean-shutdown energy | 10–15 s × 4 W ÷ 0.85 converter efficiency ≈ 50–70 J |
| Crank-bridge energy | 1–3 s × 5 W ≈ 5–15 J |
| Two 2.7 V cells in series, 10 F total, charged to about 5 V | ½·C·V² ≈ 125 J stored; about 105 J usable above a 2 V converter floor, about 20 s at 4 W |
| Charge time from empty at a 1 A budget | 10 F × 5 V ÷ 1 A ≈ 50 s; slower on a 1.5 A source that is also running the Pi |

before the radios' draw is counted. `powerspec` replaces every row with a measurement and
states the margin.

**Limits, stated plainly.**

- **Cold start.** The bank is empty at the first key-on of a session, so it cannot bridge
  that crank dip, and the Pi may reset while cranking. That is survivable only because
  storage is crash-consistent. Crank bridging is best-effort; the key-off shutdown is the
  reliable path.
- **Always-live sources are not supported.** On a charger that stays live with the key
  off, the box stays on, and the Pi plus the dongle can drain the car's battery over a few
  days. This is an installation requirement, not a mode we engineer around, but whether
  the box should halt itself after a long stretch with the engine silent is open
  (`shutfsm`).
- **Weak sources.** A charger that advertises only default USB current (500 or 900 mA)
  cannot run a Pi 4 with both radios, and the bank cannot make up the difference for a
  whole drive. What the box does then (refuse to start and show red, or run degraded) is
  open (`powerspec`).
- **Boot time.** A stock Pi 4 boots in roughly half a minute (estimate, `bootbudget`), so
  the start of each drive's warm-up goes unrecorded.
- **Demo day.** The box is off unless powered, and the handout's live demonstration runs
  on live sensors (§5, §11), so the demo needs a running testbed car on site, or an
  arrangement with the professor (`democar`).

  current is measured before it stays plugged in overnight (`dongledrain`).

P13): "no need to reinvent the charger." The owner already has a USB-C charger, so the
team designs the box and buys only the dongle and a cable. One port and one light is a
product an ordinary owner can install.

**Why a supercapacitor.** Camden's choice, 2026-10-21 (R1). A lithium cell must not
charge above about 45 °C or below 0 °C, and a car cabin leaves that window at both ends;
many cheap Pi UPS boards have no temperature cutoff. A supercapacitor has no
thermal-runaway failure, tolerates a wider temperature range (confirm against the part's
datasheet), and fits a seconds-scale job. Its costs are low voltage per cell (two in
series, with balancing), very low internal resistance (so a fuse), and fast
self-discharge, which does not matter for a box that is off at rest.

before power loss, so every key-off cut a write. A small lithium cell: the charge
temperature window above. A wake button: dropped (P10).

path (`powerspec`, `schpower`, `capbench`), and more to measure before any claim

### A.7 — Standard Mode 01 requests are the primary data path ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-012` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude
· **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

*Revised 2026-09-21 by D-015, before any review: the CAN-level detail (arbitration IDs,
broadcast frames, a listen-only flag, the port-traffic check) went with the MCP2515.*

**Decision.** The capture daemon gets its signals by sending **standard OBD2 Mode 01
requests** through the OBD2 adapter (D-019) on a fixed, rate-limited, round-robin schedule,
one request outstanding at a time. Every timeout and every unanswered PID is logged.

**Why.** D-011 (now D-024) makes this a plug-in device, and the thing that makes a plug-in
device work on a car it has never seen is the part of the protocol every car must speak:
Mode 01 is mandatory on US cars from model year 1996. *"Learns this car's normal"* is
precisely what lets one device serve different cars without per-model decode work: it
never needs to know what normal *is* ahead of time.

**Sample-rate consequence.** Signals are round-robined, so each PID is sampled at
(request rate ÷ PID count) — on the order of 1 Hz each for a ~10 requests/s budget over
~8 PIDs. That is ample for what we watch (warm-up over minutes, fuel trim against load,
drift over days) and must be stated in `docs/DESIGN.md` §4. The request budget itself
is a design-doc number to justify, not a constant to pick.

**Cost.** The device sends requests to the car's ECU. Kept safe by the rate limit, one
outstanding request, and only standard read-only Mode 01 requests — the same thing every
scan tool does.

**Scope note.** "Works on any car" is the product's direction, not our claim. The claim is
E.1 (D-021): one car, a learned normal, fault areas named, measured error rates.

### A.8 — A real-time clock keeps wall time while the box is off ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-030` · Decided M2, 2026-10-21 · **By:** Camden (in session) + Claude
· **Reviewed:** Camden ⬜ / Lance ⬜

**Decision.** The box gets a small real-time clock module on the Pi's I2C bus, kept
running by its own backup cell or capacitor while the box is off. At boot the system
clock is set from it. If the clock reports its time as invalid (its backup was lost),
that session's wall time is marked untrusted. Every record still carries `mono_ns`
regardless. The phone page stays read-only: it does not set the clock.

**Why.** The Pi has no battery-backed clock, and the box has no network (`CLAUDE.md`
§2.3). Raspberry Pi OS's `fake-hwclock` restores the time saved at the last shutdown, so
the clock does not advance while the box is off, and every boot would appear to follow the
previous shutdown directly. The soak (D-023) must prove a 48-hour wall-clock span across
parked gaps, and the report's session list needs real times. Camden chose the clock
module, 2026-10-21, over the phone setting the time (that depends on someone opening the
page on every drive) and over no wall clock at all (`docs/REVISION_PLAN.md` §1.2, R5).

**Cost.**

- One more part, on I2C (GPIO2 and GPIO3, header pins 3 and 5), drawn in the Pi interface
  block, and bought only after the design is signed.
- Its backup cell or capacitor lives in a parked car's cabin, so its temperature rating
  must cover that, checked against the part's datasheet (`rtcspec`).

  boot path checks it (`rtcboot`).

## B. Systems architecture and mechanisms

### B.1 — Mechanism commitments: D and E; B and F only with a Pi-side sensor ⚠️ UNREVIEWED

`D-017` · Decided M1, 2026-09-21 · **By:** Camden + Claude
· **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜
· **Supersedes:** D-002 (§G.3)

*B and F declined 2026-10-21 by D-029 (§B.7), before any review: no Pi-side sensor will be
added, so D and E are the committed pair and the "only if" rows below no longer apply.*

The handout requires two, implemented by us and measured.

| Mechanism | Status | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **D** — custom append-only storage, crash-consistent | **committed** | `src/store/` |
| **E** — multi-process with a supervisor | **committed** | `src/supervisor/`, `src/ipc/` |
| **B** — interrupt-driven input with a polling comparison | declined (D-029) | — |
| **F** — high-rate no-drop SPSC ring | declined (D-029) | — |
| **A**, **C**, raw CAN | stretch, after D and E are measured | — |

**D.** *Power disappears every time the key turns off* (D-024). The box shuts down
cleanly on its supercapacitor when it can, but the bank is empty at a cold start, a
pulled cable beats it, and a crank dip can reset the Pi, so storage must survive a cut at
any instant. *(Revised 2026-10-21 by D-024; it read "we never get a clean shutdown".)*
Measured by cutting the Pi's own 5 V rail mid-write, after the converter so the
supercapacitor cannot cover it, repeatedly, and proving recovery (`expcrash`). Pulling
the charger no longer tests this: it triggers a clean shutdown.

**E.** A recorder that dies silently has actively harmed its user, who believes it is on
duty. Any child may be `kill -9`'d; the system degrades, logs, recovers. Measured by killing
each child repeatedly and timing detection and recovery (`expkill`).

**Why B and F left the OBD data path (D-015, D-019).** B needs an interrupt that *our*
design services. The adapter's interrupts belong to the kernel's Bluetooth and RFCOMM
stack; our process only blocks on a tty, and at ~10–20 replies/s a poll loop keeps up
trivially — the comparison would measure the tty layer, not a design of ours. F needs a
*high-rate* stream; ~10–20 samples/s never stresses a ring, so "zero drops under
contention" would be true and meaningless.

**What brings them back.** An MPU-6050 on the Pi's I2C, its `INT` pin on a GPIO: kHz
samples from a hardware FIFO give a real interrupt-vs-polling comparison (B) and a rate
that stresses the ring (F). That was board item `pisensor`; D-029 declined it.

**The ring stays regardless.** It is how capture hands samples to storage across the
process boundary E requires, and B.3 still binds it.

**Risk.** D and E alone meet the floor exactly. If either measurement fails, nothing is in
reserve. `pisensor` was that reserve, and D-029 declined it.

### B.2 — Four processes, not one 🔒

`D-002` (corollary) · **By:** Camden + Claude · **Reviewed:** Camden ✅ / Lance ⬜

`obdd`, `storaged`, `analyzed` and `supervisor` are separate processes with separate
address spaces, communicating over a shared-memory ring and Unix domain sockets.

**Why.** Fault isolation is the product requirement, not an architectural preference: the
analysis engine is the most complex and least trustworthy component, and it must not be
able to take the capture path down with it. One process would be simpler and would fail
the thing the device exists to do.
