# Schematic conventions

**Owner:** unclaimed (D-026). The KiCad project lives in `electricalDrawing/`.
`make hwcheck` must pass before any PR touching it is opened.

## Scope: schematic yes, PCB probably no

**Decision A.4 in `docs/DECISIONS.md`.** We capture the schematic; we do not fabricate a
board unless we take The Reach (handout §14).

A custom PCB earns **zero points** — the rubric grades mechanisms, measurements and the
soak — and adds fab turnaround on top of the hardware critical path (`docs/PLAN.md` §1),
which M2 has already overrun. Off-the-shelf parts on a breadboard clear every guardrail,
and the handout is explicit that the enclosure can be a food container.

The schematic is worth the time anyway, because three graded artifacts depend on it:

- `docs/DESIGN.md` needs an architecture diagram and a defensible wiring story
- `docs/hardware/wiring.md` needs pin assignments that cannot drift from reality
- The **three-isolated-workers test** needs a parts-only buyer who can order from the BOM
  without ever seeing the design

`electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.kicad_pcb` stays in the repo, empty, on purpose. Its
emptiness is a recorded position, not an oversight.

## Sheet structure

Lance has blocked out functional areas on the root sheet. Keep that shape; it maps onto the
architecture, which makes both documents easier to defend:

| Block | Contains |
| --- | --- |
| **Power** | The box's USB-C sink input (5.1 kΩ on CC1 and CC2) as an off-sheet connector; input protection and fuse; current limit and inrush limiter; the supercapacitor bank with balancing and its fuse; the power-path controller; the step-up-capable 5 V / 3 A converter to the Pi; the source-present and halt-done signals (D-024). **No** OBD2 pin 16. |
| **Pi interface** | 40-pin header, the tri-color LED with its resistors and the pull that holds yellow on during boot (D-027), source-present (divided to 3.3 V) and halt-done GPIOs, the real-time clock on I2C (D-030), the DS18B20 probe connector on GPIO4 with its 4.7 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V (D-037), grounds |
| **CAN** *(stretch only, D-019)* | OBD2 pin 6 / pin 14 / pin 5 via the Y-splitter, TJA1050 transceiver, MCP2515, crystal + load caps, termination jumper **drawn open** (nothing on the car is disturbed, D-024), `INT` to GPIO, SPI0 (CE0/MISO/MOSI/SCLK) |

The OBD2 adapter is not on the schematic: it plugs into the car and reaches the Pi over
Bluetooth (D-019), so no wire of ours touches it.

## Rules

1. **Every net that leaves a block is a named label**, not a wire crossing a boundary. The
   netlist is read by humans at the defense.
2. **Annotate the voltage domain on every power net** (`+5V_USB`, `+V_BANK`, `+5V`,
   `+3V3`). The Pi has no 5 V-tolerant inputs and no over-voltage protection; a mislabeled
   rail is how a Pi dies silently in Week 13.
3. **Every IC gets its decoupling drawn**, even when the module already has it. The
   schematic documents what is *electrically true*, not what we happened to buy assembled.
4. *(CAN stretch only.)* **The MCP2515 crystal frequency is a value field, not a comment**
   — 8 MHz vs 16 MHz changes the device-tree overlay, and a wrong value produces a
   silently dead bus.
5. **No `DNP`/`no-connect` without a reason in the field.** Floating inputs are an ERC
   violation for good reasons.
6. **`make hwcheck` green before the PR.** ERC violations are build failures, exactly like
   `-Werror`.

## What must not be trusted to a datasheet alone

*Applies only if the CAN stretch goal is taken up.* The cheap MCP2515 breakout modules
vary: some run the TJA1050 at 5 V and level-shift the controller side, and some do not —
those drive **5 V onto MISO** and will kill a Pi.

**Meter it. With the Pi disconnected. Before anything is plugged in.** This is the exact
case `CLAUDE.md` §8.4 covers: no hardware conclusion from a verbal description or a
datasheet, on a board nobody has measured. Record the measured voltages in
`docs/hardware/wiring.md` with the date.

## Generated, never hand-edited

`make hwdocs` regenerates these from the schematic. If a pin table and the schematic
disagree, the schematic wins and the table was stale:

- `docs/figures/electricalDrawing.svg` — rendered schematic, **committed**, so pull requests
  show a picture instead of an S-expression diff
- `docs/hardware/bom.csv` — the parts list `BOM.md` is checked against
- `electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.net` — the netlist `wiring.md`'s pin tables are
  checked against

None of them exists yet: nothing has been drawn (`schpower`, `schpi`). `BOM.md` and
`wiring.md` are written by hand, by function, and stay that way; once a block is drawn,
the PR that draws it checks them against `bom.csv` and the netlist (`hwgate`).

19	- `docs/hardware/wiring.md` needs pin assignments that cannot drift from reality
20	- The **three-isolated-workers test** needs a parts-only buyer who can order from the BOM
21	  without ever seeing the design
22	
23	`electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.kicad_pcb` stays in the repo, empty, on purpose. Its
24	emptiness is a recorded position, not an oversight.
25	
26	## Sheet structure
27	
28	Lance has blocked out functional areas on the root sheet. Keep that shape; it maps onto the
29	architecture, which makes both documents easier to defend:
30	
31	| Block | Contains |
32	| --- | --- |
33	| **Power** | The box's USB-C sink input (5.1 kΩ on CC1 and CC2) as an off-sheet connector; input protection and fuse; current limit and inrush limiter; the supercapacitor bank with balancing and its fuse; the power-path controller; the step-up-capable 5 V / 3 A converter to the Pi; the source-present and halt-done signals (D-024). **No** OBD2 pin 16. |
34	| **Pi interface** | 40-pin header, the tri-color LED with its resistors and the pull that holds yellow on during boot (D-027), source-present (divided to 3.3 V) and halt-done GPIOs, the real-time clock on I2C (D-030), the DS18B20 probe connector on GPIO4 with its 4.7 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V (D-037), grounds |
35	| **CAN** *(stretch only, D-019)* | OBD2 pin 6 / pin 14 / pin 5 via the Y-splitter, TJA1050 transceiver, MCP2515, crystal + load caps, termination jumper **drawn open** (nothing on the car is disturbed, D-024), `INT` to GPIO, SPI0 (CE0/MISO/MOSI/SCLK) |
36	
37	The OBD2 adapter is not on the schematic: it plugs into the car and reaches the Pi over
38	Bluetooth (D-019), so no wire of ours touches it.
39	
40	## Rules
41	
42	1. **Every net that leaves a block is a named label**, not a wire crossing a boundary. The
43	   netlist is read by humans at the defense.
44	2. **Annotate the voltage domain on every power net** (`+5V_USB`, `+V_BANK`, `+5V`,
45	   `+3V3`). The Pi has no 5 V-tolerant inputs and no over-voltage protection; a mislabeled
46	   rail is how a Pi dies silently in Week 13.
47	3. **Every IC gets its decoupling drawn**, even when the module already has it. The
48	   schematic documents what is *electrically true*, not what we happened to buy assembled.
49	4. *(CAN stretch only.)* **The MCP2515 crystal frequency is a value field, not a comment**
50	   — 8 MHz vs 16 MHz changes the device-tree overlay, and a wrong value produces a
51	   silently dead bus.
52	5. **No `DNP`/`no-connect` without a reason in the field.** Floating inputs are an ERC
53	   violation for good reasons.
54	6. **`make hwcheck` green before the PR.** ERC violations are build failures, exactly like
55	   `-Werror`.
56	
57	## What must not be trusted to a datasheet alone
58	
59	*Applies only if the CAN stretch goal is taken up.* The cheap MCP2515 breakout modules
60	vary: some run the TJA1050 at 5 V and level-shift the controller side, and some do not —
61	those drive **5 V onto MISO** and will kill a Pi.
62	
63	**Meter it. With the Pi disconnected. Before anything is plugged in.** This is the exact
64	case `CLAUDE.md` §8.4 covers: no hardware conclusion from a verbal description or a
65	datasheet, on a board nobody has measured. Record the measured voltages in
66	`docs/hardware/wiring.md` with the date.
67	
68	## Generated, never hand-edited
69	
70	`make hwdocs` regenerates these from the schematic. If a pin table and the schematic
71	disagree, the schematic wins and the table was stale:
72	
73	- `docs/figures/electricalDrawing.svg` — rendered schematic, **committed**, so pull requests
74	  show a picture instead of an S-expression diff
75	- `docs/hardware/bom.csv` — the parts list `BOM.md` is checked against
76	- `electricalDrawing/electricalDrawing.net` — the netlist `wiring.md`'s pin tables are
77	  checked against
78	
79	None of them exists yet: nothing has been drawn (`schpower`, `schpi`). `BOM.md` and
80	`wiring.md` are written by hand, by function, and stay that way; once a block is drawn,
81	the PR that draws it checks them against `bom.csv` and the netlist (`hwgate`).
82

# Evaluation report — carwatch

> **STATUS: M5 SKELETON.** 3–4 pages. "Adjectives are not measurements."
> Claude can generate plausible code; it cannot fake your understanding of your own
> measurements — which is why the defense draws so heavily on this document. Every
> number in here must be one you can reproduce while someone watches.

## 1. Method and setup

Hardware, kernel version, build flags, what was running, how load was generated,
how many trials. Enough for a TA to re-measure.

**Every figure states whether its data is live, replay, or synth.** No exceptions.

## 2. Latency / timing
>
> Distributions, not just means. Under both idle and loaded CPU.

- OBD reply arrival (tty read) → durable in the log: p50 / p95 / p99 / max, idle and loaded
- Histogram, not a table of means. [figure]

## 3. Resource footprint
>
> CPU and RSS per process, at steady state and **over the full soak**. The hourly
> heartbeats give you this series for free — plot it.

Every heartbeat carries each process's RSS and its `utime` + `stime` from
`/proc/<pid>/stat`, so CPU is a series too, idle and under a CPU hog.

[figure: RSS vs. time, all processes, every session of the 48 h key-cycle window (D-023)]

A flat line here is the whole point. A device that leaks for 48 hours and happens not
to die has not passed the soak; it has outrun it.

## 4. Domain metric
>
> The one the product lives or dies by.

Detection against the ground truth we constructed (D-021): for each induced fault, was it
flagged, how fast, and was the fault area named right, as a confusion matrix over fault
areas, with the false-positive rate called out
separately because a monitor that cries wolf twice gets unplugged.

## 5. Fault-injection results
>
> For each failure mode in the design document's table: what we injected, what the
> system did, and **the log excerpt proving it**.

One row per failure-table row (`docs/DESIGN.md` §4). A row that cannot be injected says
why, here.

| Failure (DESIGN §4) | How we inject it | Expected event | Observed | Light (D-027) | Log excerpt |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bluetooth drops | pull the dongle for 10 min, engine running | `link_lost`, `reconnected` | | | |
| Garbage or timeouts | `obdsim` serving bad replies (`synth`) | `reply_bad`, `adapter_reset` | | | |
| Engine off, key in ACC | key to ACC | `ecu_silent` | | | |
| A sensor unplugged | unplug one engine sensor, engine running (lights the CEL) | `pid_absent` or `pid_flat`, `mil_on`, `pid_present` | | | |
| Probe unplugged | pull the DS18B20 for 10 min | `sensor_absent`, `sensor_present` | | | |
| A child crashes | `kill -9` each child, 20 times | `child_exit`, `child_restart` | | | |
| Ring consumer stalls | `SIGSTOP` `storaged` for 5 min | `ring_full`, `heartbeat_late` | | | |
| Power cut mid-write | cut the Pi's 5 V rail after the converter | `recovered` | | | |
| Disk full; `fsync` error | log directory on a small loop-mounted filesystem, filled | `enospc`, `fsync_failed` | | | |
| Torn checkpoint; bad model | truncate one checkpoint slot; corrupt the model header | `checkpoint_bad`, `model_unavailable` | | | |
| Report fails | make the report directory read-only | `report_failed` | | | |
| Supervisor dies | `kill -9` the supervisor | systemd restart, in the journal | | | |
| Clock invalid | remove the clock's backup, then boot | `rtc_invalid` | | | |
| Key-off, cable pulled, crank, source back | key cycles; pull the USB-C; return it during shutdown | `source_lost`, `source_dip`, `shutdown` | | | |
| Empty bank at a cold crank | cold start with the bank discharged | `recovered` | | | |
| Undervoltage, heat | a weak charger; a closed car in the sun | `undervoltage`, `thermal` | | | |
| Bluetooth and Wi-Fi share a radio | phone on the access point during a drive | reply p99 in the heartbeat | | | |

## 6. Mechanism comparisons
>
> Required by our menu choices. Present as experiments: method, data, conclusion.

### 6.1 Crash consistency (mechanism D)

N power-cut trials, each cutting the Pi's 5 V rail after the converter so the supercapacitor
cannot cover it: recovery outcome each time, bytes lost per trial.

### 6.2 Supervision (mechanism E)

`kill -9` each child N times: time to detection, time to recovery, what degraded in the
meantime, and proof that no file descriptor leaked across the restart.

### 6.3 Write batching and `fsync` discipline (mechanism D, `expbatch`)

The same `synth` stream through `storaged` on the Pi's SD card with one `fsync` per record,
per second (D-035) and per ten seconds: `fsync` latency p50 / p99, bytes written (from
`/sys/block/mmcblk0/stat`), and records lost per power cut. The conclusion says whether
D-035's one second was the right choice.

Mechanisms B and F were declined (D-029, D-037), so they have no comparison here.

## 7. Limitations

> Plainly. Closes the loop on the constraints and substitutions declared in
> docs/DESIGN.md §7.

"An honest limitations section is worth more at the defense than a suspiciously perfect
results section, and we notice which one we are reading."

Name at minimum: the fault areas we could not induce, what results on one testbed car say
(and do not say) about the other (D-022), how many weeks of normal the baseline actually
covers, and every place a number came from replay rather than live driving.

# CI for the systems core (CLAUDE.md §1): a change is done only when make, make test and
# make asan pass. This runs them with gcc and glibc on 64-bit Arm Linux, the Pi's
# architecture, so a Mac-only build (Apple clang) is never the only evidence.
#
# valgrind (make memcheck) and anything that needs the car or the adapter stay on the Pi.
####
name: build

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  core:
    name: make, make test, make asan (gcc, arm64 Linux)
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - name: make
        run: make
      - name: make test
        run: make test
      - name: make asan
        run: make asan

# Plan: fix every stale reference and bug, and close the rubric risks

## Context

A full audit on 2026-10-26 (four parallel read-only auditors plus my own checks) found three kinds of problem:

- **Stale references** to superseded decisions. Most of them come from DESIGN.md renumbering its sections.
- **Real bugs** in the build, the ring buffer and the Python tools.
- **Rubric risks:**
  - §3.1, two physically distinct sensors;
  - mechanism E's wording ("sensors isolated in separate processes");
  - a `make boundary` check that will block the Unix sockets the design needs;
  - an evaluation plan missing CPU, fsync batching and per-row fault injection;
  - DESIGN.md holes (retention, the verdict path, the IPC spec, the status-page process);
  - a README a TA cannot run;
  - soak logs that are git-ignored;
  - M3, due 2026-11-01, needs a real pipeline, and every daemon is still a stub.

Your decisions (2026-10-26):

1. Lance's contribution level is out of scope.
2. The soak definition (D-023) is already confirmed by the professor, so record it and move on.
3. Add a **DS18B20 probe**. This reopens D-029 and closes both §3.1 and the E wording.
4. Scope is **everything, including the M3 C pipeline**.

Outcome: every risk that code or docs can close is closed. What remains is human-only work (signatures, ticks, drives, purchases), listed at the end.

## Ground rules for execution (CLAUDE.md)

- **Branches.** Branches stack in a line, so the decision IDs and the DECISIONS.md review queue never conflict. Each PR is a draft, states its base branch, and is merged by a human in order.
- **Commits.** One commit has one responsibility. Every commit passes `make`, `make test` and `make asan`, and that output is pasted into the PR. Tests go in the same commit as the behavior they test.
- **Decisions.**
  - Every new decision goes into DECISIONS.md as ⚠️ UNREVIEWED and into the review queue, in the same commit as the code that enacts it.
  - 🔒 entries get dated *notes* only, flagged in the PR. They are never rewritten.
- **The board.**
  - Claude never ticks decision, question or hardware lines. The PRs list which lines a human should tick or cut.
  - New board lines are added by editing `docs/milestones.md`, then running `python tools/board_sync.py`.
- **Files Claude leaves alone.**
  - The staged transcript `.jsonl`, which you commit yourself under rule 7.1.5.
  - `partners/lance/*`.
- **Decision IDs reserved, in stack order:**

  | ID | Subject |
  | --- | --- |
  | D-037 | DS18B20 |
  | D-038 | boundary rule |
  | D-039 | ring in shared memory |
  | D-040 | `src` encoding and labeling |
  | D-041 | retention |
  | D-042 | verdict and event path |
  | D-043 | supervisor protocol, `obdctl` verbs, status-page process |
  | D-044 | ECU identity and fast-PID cadence |
  | D-045 | soak evidence location |

## Phase 1: DESIGN.md rubric alignment

Branch: `camden/m2/design-doc`, the existing branch. Open a new draft PR to `main` first: #166's work is stranded off `main`.

Commits:

1. **docs: record the professor's confirmation of D-023.**
   - E.3 "Pending" becomes "confirmed, reported by Camden 2026-10-26".
   - Update the DESIGN §7 soak row.
   - The PR asks you to tick #131 and cut #7.
2. **docs: D-037, add a DS18B20 cabin and ambient probe in its own process.**
   - **Decision content:**
     - Reopens D-029 and amends D-031: a second SPSC ring, `ambientd` → `storaged`.
     - Amends D-034: sample `mode` 0x00 is the namespace for Pi-side sensors, with pid 0x01 = DS18B20 °C.
     - Wiring follows the standard 1-Wire setup: 4.7 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V, `dtoverlay=w1-gpio`, on a GPIO checked as free against wiring.md.
   - **What the probe cooperates in:**
     - A cold-soak cross-check: after a long soak, coolant, intake air temperature and the probe must agree. This feeds the sensor/electrical area.
     - The ambient input to cooling when PID 0x46 is absent.
   - **Doc updates in the same commit:**
     - DESIGN §1 (process and ring), §2 (E becomes literal; transducer-level §3.1 defense; defines "both sensors alive / through the pipeline"), §3 rows, §4 rows (device missing, CRC `NO`, the 85000 power-on value), §6 parts.
     - BOM.md, wiring.md, the PROBLEM.md sensors heading (submitted "as revised"), the README hardware section.
     - New board lines: order the probe (hardware), bench bring-up with a pasted `w1_slave` read (hardware), and `ambientd` (M3).
3. **docs: complete the evaluation plan.** Amends draft D-036 in place, with a note.
   - Per-process CPU, from `/proc/<pid>/stat` utime and stime in the heartbeat, idle and loaded.
   - `expbatch`.
   - Probe-unplug detection.
   - A fault-injection table with one row per failure-table row, or the reason a row can't be injected.
   - Mirror the rows into EVALUATION.md §5–6.
4. **docs: failure-table fixes.**
   - Sensor unplug is detected by flat or pinned values plus the MIL and DTC count (PID 0101, Mode 03), not just `NO DATA`; note that this fault lights the check-engine light.
   - Light wording: "any other steady light".
   - One rate range throughout: 10–25 samples/s.
5. **docs: D-041 retention (#157, draft).**
   - Raw segments are kept until the disk is 80 % full, then deleted oldest-first, whole segments only.
   - Checkpoints are never deleted.
   - The doc states how many days of driving fit on the card.
   - Fills DESIGN §5.
6. **docs: D-042 verdict and event path (#162, draft).**
   - `analyzed` and the supervisor send events to `storaged` over a Unix socket (`SOCK_SEQPACKET`).
   - `storaged` writes them as event records in the next batch.
   - Closes D-031's open item.
7. **docs: D-043 supervisor protocol (#163, draft).**
   - Line-based request and reply over a Unix socket.
   - The five `obdctl` verbs, with their arguments fixed.
   - Names the status-page process `statusd` in `src/interface/`, for DESIGN §1 and the Makefile `DAEMONS`.
8. **docs: AI-use plan honesty (§10).** Claude drafted the §3 analysis proposal; the team decides it. The 🟨 box stays for you.
9. **docs: ownership map, evidence-only rows.**
   - Rows filled from first substantive commits: `src/store/`, `src/common/`, build, `board_sync`.
   - The rest stay unclaimed under 🟨 for the team.
10. **docs: tighten DESIGN.md to ≤ 5 rendered pages,** excluding the review box. Render with pandoc if it is available; otherwise estimate from word count.

## Phase 2: stale-reference sweep

Branch: `camden/m2/stale-refs`, from Phase 1. One docs commit per area:

1. **DESIGN section references** in CLAUDE.md, docs/README, DECISIONS, EVALUATION and pid-survey:
   - §7 → §9 (ownership)
   - §6 → §8 (evaluation)
   - §4 → §5 (storage)
   - §3 → §4 (failure table)
   - §5 → §7 (constraints)
   - §4 → §3 (sensor table, pid-survey only)

   Code comments are fixed when Phase 4 rewrites those files.
2. **DECISIONS entry bodies:**
   - D-019's power wording.
   - The B.1 title and the D-017, D-007 and D-013 queue rows.
   - The pointer telling Lance what to read.
   - C.3 sizes: note D-034.
   - G.2 → §G.6.
   - Dated notes on 🔒 A.4, A.5 and C.1.
3. **DECISIONS reorder (move only, labeled):** the B section into numeric order, and the review queue sorted by ID.
4. **PLAN.md:**
   - State the M2 slip.
   - Critical-path chain becomes `order` → `firstcap` → `baseline`/`pilogger`.
   - Remove the Ready/Backlog text.
5. **REVISION_PLAN.md:** freeze it with a HISTORICAL banner. Its still-open items become board lines.
6. **Hardware docs:**

- ELM init.
- Read the supported-PID bitmap.
- Round-robin requests with one outstanding, using D-044's cadence.
- A C parser and decode table, checked against golden vectors generated from `tools/obdlib.py`.
- Reconnect with backoff.
- Absent-PID logic per the failure table.
- Heartbeat.
- `--src` cross-checked against the adapter banner (D-040): refuse `live` if the banner says SIM or REPLAY.
- Integration test in `tests/tools`: `obdsim` pty → `obdd` → `storaged` → records labeled `synth`.

### `ambientd` (new board line)

- Reads `/sys/bus/w1/devices/28-*/w1_slave` every 2 s, with a `--sysfs-root` option so tests can use a fake tree.
- Rejects a CRC `NO` and the 85000 power-on value.
- Logs `sensor_absent` and `sensor_present`.
- Feeds ring 2.

### Supervisor (#41, #42, #43)

- `fork`/`exec`, with `O_CLOEXEC` throughout and `waitpid`.
- Restart with backoff and a storm guard.
- Creates the rings.
- Orderly SIGTERM.
- Every daemon heartbeats within 60 s and hourly, with RSS, CPU and counts.
- The light is driven as logged state only, until the hardware exists (#89).

### `obdctl status` (#44)

`src/ipc/uds.c` (`AF_UNIX` only), the D-043 protocol, and the `status` verb.

### Replay (#45, #160)

- `replay.py` serves a JSONL capture on a pty with its recorded timing, reusing `obdsim`'s pty code, with banner REPLAY.
- The label comes from the input: `live` becomes `replay`, `synth` stays `synth`, mixed input is refused. No `--label` flag.
- `make replay FIX=` runs the real pipeline into a temp log.

### Soak harness (#46)

- `run_soak.sh --mini`: supervisor plus `obdsim` labeled `synth`, a `kill -9` mid-run, and assertions that the log shows heartbeats, `child_restart`, `recovered` and a flat RSS. Also runs on the asan build.
- Fix the argument parsing.
- D-045: graded soak runs land in `soak/evidence/`, which is committed; `soak/logs/` stays scratch.

### Install, provision and the TA path

- `install.sh` writes a systemd unit for the supervisor with `Restart=always`.
- `provision_pi.sh`:
  - Check for a 64-bit OS.
  - Install packages.
  - `rfcomm bind` with the adapter's MAC as an argument.
  - A udev rule for `/dev/obd`.
  - The w1-gpio and RTC overlays.
  - Disable `fake-hwclock`.

  Both scripts are marked "untested on hardware", with a bench board line.
- README gets a "TA mode, no car": `make && make soakcheck` runs the whole pipeline on `obdsim`, labeled `synth`.

## Reuse

- `tools/obdsim.py`: the pty ELM emulator, for `obdd` integration tests and replay.
- `tools/obdlib.py`: the PID table and parser, as golden vectors for the C decoder.
- `obdsum`'s all-records `src` check.
- `src/store/crc32.c` and its known-answer test.
- `src/common/log.c`: heartbeat, extended with CPU.
- `src/ipc/ring.c`: semantics kept (refuse, never overwrite, B.3).
- The scratchpad stress test.

## Verification

- **Every commit:** `make`, `make test` and `make asan` green, pasted in the PR. The Linux arm64 CI job is green once it exists.
- **Docs commits:** markdownlint-cli2 and cspell from the npx cache are clean on touched files. `python tools/test_board.py` passes. `board_sync.py --check` before the real sync.
- **Mechanism D:** the every-byte-cut recovery test plus `storaged` `kill -9` tests show no committed record lost.
- **Mechanism E:** `soakcheck --mini` with `kill -9` of each child, showing detection, restart and no fd growth (`ls /proc/<pid>/fd` on Linux CI).
- **Pipeline:** `obdsim` → `obdd` → ring → `storaged` → log, decoded and labeled `synth`; replay of the synth fixture is labeled correctly; probe tests run against the fake sysfs tree.
- **Boundary:** the `tests/boundary/` fixtures must fail the check, and the real tree must pass.

## What only you (or Lance) can do afterwards

These keep a risk open until a human acts.

1. Sign or alter D-019 to D-045.
2. Tick or cut the board lines each PR lists.
3. Merge the PRs in stack order.
4. Run the first Forester drive and both PID surveys, and paste the evidence.
5. Buy and bench the DS18B20 and the power-block parts.
6. Decide the §3 fault rows and the unclaimed ownership rows.
7. Replace 📏 with drive numbers and delete the review box.
8. Write the PROMPTLOG judgment paragraphs; E-02 is cited by G.4 and G.6.
9. Commit the transcripts, including the staged one.
10. Render the PDF and submit M2 (#161).
11. Arrange the M3 checkpoint venue with a running car.


If this plan is relevant to the current work and not already complete, continue working on it.
</system-reminder>

- engineering:architecture: Create or evaluate an architecture decision record (ADR). Use when choosing between technologies (e.g., Kafka vs SQS), documenting a design decision with trade-offs and consequences, reviewing a system design proposal, or designing a new component from requirements and constraints.
- engineering:code-review: Review code changes for security, performance, and correctness. Trigger with a PR URL or diff, "review this before I merge", "is this code safe?", or when checking a change for N+1 queries, injection risks, missing edge cases, or error handling gaps.
- engineering:debug: Structured debugging session — reproduce, isolate, diagnose, and fix. Trigger with an error message or stack trace, "this works in staging but not prod", "something broke after the deploy", or when behavior diverges from expected and the cause isn't obvious.
- engineering:deploy-checklist: Pre-deployment verification checklist. Use when about to ship a release, deploying a change with database migrations or feature flags, verifying CI status and approvals before going to production, or documenting rollback triggers ahead of time.
- engineering:documentation: Write and maintain technical documentation. Trigger with "write docs for", "document this", "create a README", "write a runbook", "onboarding guide", or when the user needs help with any form of technical writing — API docs, architecture docs, or operational runbooks.
- engineering:incident-response: Run an incident response workflow — triage, communicate, and write postmortem. Trigger with "we have an incident", "production is down", an alert that needs severity assessment, a status update mid-incident, or when writing a blameless postmortem after resolution.
- engineering:standup: Generate a standup update from recent activity. Use when preparing for daily standup, summarizing yesterday's commits and PRs and ticket moves, formatting work into yesterday/today/blockers, or structuring a few rough notes into a shareable update.
- engineering:system-design: Design systems, services, and architectures. Trigger with "design a system for", "how should we architect", "system design for", "what's the right architecture for", or when the user needs help with API design, data modeling, or service boundaries.
- engineering:tech-debt: Identify, categorize, and prioritize technical debt. Trigger with "tech debt", "technical debt audit", "what should we refactor", "code health", or when the user asks about code quality, refactoring priorities, or maintenance backlog.
- engineering:testing-strategy: Design test strategies and test plans. Trigger with "how should we test", "test strategy for", "write tests for", "test plan", "what tests do we need", or when the user needs help with testing approaches, coverage, or test architecture.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, handing the viewer a file to save, or using the viewer's camera, microphone, location, screen or device motion. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever any such runtime behavior would make an artifact more useful, before writing the page.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. Pass --max-findings <n> to report up to n findings, or --max-findings all for every finding. The choice stays until you pass --max-findings default. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. **IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list).
